title: Shiva's eyes stay closed
hookLine: Kama brings spring to the mountain to break Shiva's meditation, and the whole forest falls in love except the yogi
carry: pratyahara: settle the mind, and the senses follow
last: PRANA: SLOW BREATH THINS THE VEIL.

cards: High in the Himalayas, Shiva sits in meditation. Eyes half closed, breath slow, still as a lamp in a place with no wind.
The gods need him to wake and marry Parvati, so they send Kama, the god of desire, with his bow and his arrows of flowers. Kama brings spring with him, out of season.
In the poet Kalidasa's telling, the whole forest goes soft with longing: trees burst into bloom, bees hum, animals pair off.
Then Nandi, Shiva's attendant, raises a finger to his lips, and the forest freezes, still as a painting. Shiva's eyes stay closed.

teach.b: Parvati comes with flowers for him, and Kama draws his bow. For a moment, the poem says, Shiva's calm stirs, like the ocean when the moon rises. He opens his eyes, looks for the cause, and sees Kama, bow drawn.
Fire leaps from Shiva's third eye, and the god of desire falls to ash. The Shiva Purana tells it too.
This is why Hindus picture Shiva as the great yogi, seated on the mountain with eyes half closed: the senses drawn in, the whole world blooming around him, and none of it dragging him out.
Patanjali's name for that is pratyahara, the fifth limb. Prati, back. Ahara, taking in.
Drawing back. Sutra 2.54: when the senses aren't joined to their objects, they follow the nature of the mind.
The classical commentary's picture: bees follow their leader. When the leader settles, the swarm settles. You don't chase each bee.
You settle the mind, and the senses come home. Sutra 2.55, the last line of book two: from this, supreme mastery of the senses. The Gita's image is the tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell.
Notice what Shiva burns. Not Parvati, not the spring. The pull.
Many teachers read it this way: the senses aren't enemies, and Shiva does marry Parvati later, won by her own tapas.
Pratyahara isn't hating the world. It's the mind choosing where it lives, and the senses following. So when the phone buzzes through your prayer or your homework, fighting each buzz rarely works.
Giving the mind one place to rest does.

how: In yoga practice, pratyahara is usually cultivated by resting attention on one object, such as the breath or a mantra, until the senses quiet; images of Shiva seated in meditation with eyes half closed, in temples and homes, picture it, and teachers often cite the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs.

o: fasting from food to weaken the senses
shutting your eyes and ears by sheer force
drawing the senses back as the mind settles

games.q: the fifth limb — tap the pairs.

s: pratyahara means forcing the senses to shut off
2.54: when the mind settles, the senses follow it, like bees following their leader.
in the story, Shiva's fire falls on Kama, not on Parvati or the spring
he burns the pull, desire itself.
book two of the Yoga Sutras ends with pratyahara
2.55, supreme mastery of the senses, is its last sutra.

games.q: you're saying a mantra and your phone keeps buzzing on the table. what does sutra 2.54 suggest?
o: fight each buzz until it stops bothering you.
give the mind one place to rest, and let the senses follow.
games.why: the commentary's bees follow their leader: when the mind settles, the senses settle. you don't chase each bee.

practice: Give the mind one place to rest: a mantra you know, like om namah shivaya, said softly inside, or, if you don't pray, the feeling of the breath at the tip of the nose.
Don't try to block sounds or sights; when a noise pulls you, just return. Notice whether the hearing quiets a little on its own, following the mind.

wordCard.voice: Pratyahara. The drawing back of the senses, the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses follow it home.

orig.note: Sanskrit pratyāhāra: prati (back) plus āhāra (taking in); the withdrawal of the senses, the fifth limb.

carryVoice: Your line: pratyahara: settle the mind, and the senses follow. Settle the leader, and the swarm comes home. Day four sixty-four, done.
